evidence.label: The Gaussian free field limit of the balanced six-vertex model with variance multiplier 1/arcsin(c/2)

headline: The balanced six-vertex height surface tends to a Gaussian free field for all c up to 2, with variance 1/arcsin(c/2).
scope: Weights a = b = 1 and 0 < c ≤ 2, in one zero-slope plane state built from balanced tori. Uniqueness is not claimed.
plain: The six-vertex model puts an arrow on every edge of a square grid, with two arrows in and two out at each corner. These arrows define a random height surface. Physicists predicted that, zoomed out, this surface looks like a Gaussian free field, a standard random landscape. This paper claims to prove that across the whole range 0 < c ≤ 2, with the exact strength 1/arcsin(c/2). No computer proof checker has checked it.
doesNot: This does not show the plane state is unique, or cover other slopes or the range c above 2.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Di Francesco, Saleur and Zuber, the Coulomb-gas Gaussian prediction
scorecard.significanceWhy: If it holds, it covers the whole critical range, including the endpoint c = 2, where earlier proofs covered only parts.

explanation:
Draw a square grid and put an arrow on every edge. At each corner, insist that exactly two arrows point in and two point out. That is the ice rule[1]. There are exactly six ways to satisfy it at one corner, hence the name six-vertex model. Water ice obeys the same rule for its hydrogen atoms. With every corner type weighted equally, Lieb computed the exact count in 1967. The number of grid configurations grows like about 1.540 to the power of the number of corners.

The arrows define a height. Cross an arrow, and the height on its left is one more than on its right[2]. The ice rule makes this consistent all the way round each corner. So a random arrow pattern is a random surface. The model has a weight c for the two corner types whose horizontal arrows both point in or both point out. The other four types get weight one[3].

Zoom out, and the surface should look like the Gaussian free field. That is the natural random landscape in two dimensions, where heights at two points are correlated like minus the log of their distance. The open question is its strength. The paper's answer for the squared multiplier is 1/arcsin(c/2). For c = 1 that is about 1.910. For c = √2 it is about 1.273. For c = 2 it is about 0.637. So larger c gives a flatter surface. For 1 < c < 2, a physics prediction by Di Francesco, Saleur and Zuber agrees with this formula[4].

Earlier proofs covered pieces of the range. At c = √2, the model maps to domino tilings, and Kenyon proved Gaussian free field limits there[5]. Duminil-Copin, Karrila, Manolescu and Oulamara proved logarithmic delocalization for 1 ≤ c ≤ 2. That fixes the size of fluctuations but not their joint law[6]. Duminil-Copin, Kozlowski, Lammers and Manolescu gave a Gaussian free field theorem for √3 ≤ c ≤ 2. It relies on a rotational-invariance input listed as in preparation[7].

This paper claims the limit for every c in the whole range 0 < c ≤ 2[8]. The surface comes from a plane state built from balanced tori. A torus is a grid wrapped around in both directions. Balanced means each column holds equal numbers of left and right arrows. The paper takes the width to infinity first, then the height. It says that existence of this state in the previously untreated range is part of the theorem[9].

The obstacle is getting the exact law, not just the fluctuation size. The paper builds two Gaussian currents from exact row identities of the transfer matrix, which adds one row of the grid at a time[10]. At the endpoint c = 2, it supplies the needed rotation invariance through a loop representation[11].

The claim has limits. It is about this one zero-slope plane state. It makes no uniqueness claim among all states or slopes, and nothing uniform as c shrinks to 0[12].

How sure is this? No Lean formalization is listed for this paper in the openai/math release. So no computer proof checker has checked it. No specialist review has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if it holds. It completes the critical range, but no Lean formalization is listed and no specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: Arrows on the edges of a square grid with two in and two out at every corner, weighted by corner type.
The rule that exactly two arrows enter and two leave each corner.
A number on each face of the grid, going up by one when you cross an arrow from right to left.
The standard random landscape in two dimensions, with heights correlated like minus the log of distance.
The height surface's fluctuations grow without bound, here like the log of the system size.
A matrix that builds a grid model one row at a time, so its properties give the whole model.
A grid wrapped around in both directions, so it has no edges.
